texts.title: Building a product brand
texts.body: I did not start this because I loved pool equipment. I started it because I wanted something that was mine. Here's the thing nobody tells you about building a product. The product is maybe ten percent of it. The rest is a thousand small decisions that all look identical on the day you make them. What goes on the box. What the second photo shows. Whether the hose is fifty feet or seventy five. None of those feel important. All of them decide whether it sells. I spent two months on a product page once. Two months. Photos, copy, the whole thing. And it sold about the same as it did before I touched it. What moved it, eventually, was changing the price by two dollars and fixing one line in the title. So now I try to find the two dollar decision first. Before I do the two month one. That is the part I am still learning. What about you, when you build something, do you go wide first or deep first?

texts.title: Training at the gym after work
texts.body: I get out of work around two thirty and I go straight to the gym. Not home first. Home first means I do not go. That is not discipline. That is just knowing myself. The training itself is short. Full body, three days a week, heavy, and I am out in under an hour. I used to think more was better. More days, more sets, more everything. And I got smaller. Actually smaller. Because I was training a body that never got to recover. Here's the thing I did not expect. The hardest part is not the set. The hardest part is the drive there when I am already tired from work and my brain is making a very reasonable case for tomorrow. The set is easy. I have never once regretted the set. So the whole game for me is the twelve minutes in the car. Win that and the rest happens on its own. Do you have one of those? A twelve minute thing that decides your whole day?

texts.title: Why I went back to a W-2
texts.body: People assume going back to a job means the business failed. It did not. What happened is I ran out of runway before I ran out of plan. Those are two different problems and I was solving the wrong one. When money is tight, every decision gets worse. I was pricing out of fear. I was taking deals I did not want. I was saying yes to things because a no felt expensive. So I took the job. And the thing that surprised me is that the business got better almost immediately. Not because I had more time, I have less. Because I stopped making scared decisions. Here's the thing. Everybody talks about burning the boats. Nobody talks about what happens to your judgment when you are standing on a beach with no boat. I would rather have a floor and think clearly than have no floor and make sharp moves out of panic. I do not know if that is the right call forever. It is the right call now. Where do you land on that, boats burned or boats parked?

texts.title: What I learned about saying yes to everything
texts.body: For a long stretch I said yes to basically everything. Every favor, every ask, every plan somebody else made. I thought that made me easy to be around. Generous. Low maintenance. What it actually made me was invisible. Because a guy who says yes to everything is not really in the room. He has no shape. There is nothing to push against. And it did not even work. The person I was doing it for did not feel taken care of. She felt like she was talking to somebody with no opinions, which is a lonely thing to be next to. Here's the thing I got backwards. I thought saying no would cost me the relationship. Saying yes to everything is what cost me the relationship. Now I try to say no about once a day. Small stuff. Not to be difficult, just to keep the muscle awake. And the strange part is people take it fine. Almost every time. The disaster I was avoiding was never actually there. Have you ever tested that? Said the no you were sure would blow something up?

texts.title: The sandbag
texts.body: I sell a workout sandbag. Simple product. Bag, handles, filler bags, you load it to whatever weight you want. Here's the thing about a sandbag. It is a terrible product on paper. It is heavy to ship, it is boring to photograph, and every competitor's looks exactly like it. I almost did not do it. What changed my mind was reading the reviews on everybody else's. Same complaint, over and over. The seams blow out. People were loading them to a hundred pounds and dropping them, and the stitching gave. So the entire product decision came down to one thing. Better stitching, and say so in the first line. That is it. That is the whole strategy. I did not invent anything. I read what people were already angry about and I fixed that one thing. And it works better than the products I was clever about. I keep trying to remember that. What is the boring complaint nobody has fixed yet?

texts.title: The morning trail walk
texts.body: I walk the trail in the morning. Early, before it gets hot, usually before anything else has started. No podcast, no phone call. Sometimes music, mostly not. I am not doing it for fitness. It barely counts as exercise. I am doing it because it is the only part of the day where nothing is asking me for something. Here's the thing I noticed. I get most of my actual answers out there. Not because I am thinking hard. Because I am not. The problem I have been chewing on for three days just quietly resolves itself somewhere around the halfway point. And then I get back and I write it down before it evaporates. I used to think the work happened at the desk and the walk was the break. I think I had it backwards. The walk is where the thinking happens. The desk is where I type up what I already figured out. So I protect that hour. It is not negotiable anymore. Do you have a place like that? Somewhere your head actually works?
